tests.title: Unit 1: Introduction to English Grammar – Practice Test 1

questions.question_text: Grammar is:
options: The set of rules governing how words combine to form correct sentences
questions.explanation: It covers word forms and sentence structure.

questions.question_text: The eight parts of speech are:
options: Letter, word, phrase, clause, sentence, paragraph, essay, book
Noun, pronoun, verb, adjective, adverb, preposition, conjunction and interjection
Subject, object, verb, tense, voice, mood, case, number
Noun, verb, clause, phrase, tense, voice, mood, article
questions.explanation: Every word belongs to one of these classes.

questions.question_text: A noun is a word that names:
options: A person, place, thing, animal, idea or quality
questions.explanation: Types include proper, common, collective, abstract, material, countable and uncountable nouns.

questions.question_text: A proper noun differs from a common noun in that a proper noun:
options: Names a particular person, place or thing and begins with a capital letter
questions.explanation: Delhi and Infosys are proper; city and company are common.

questions.question_text: Which is a collective noun?
questions.explanation: Team, board and jury are also collective nouns.

questions.question_text: Which is an abstract noun?
questions.explanation: Abstract nouns name qualities or ideas, like freedom and management.

questions.question_text: Which noun is uncountable?
questions.explanation: Advice, furniture, luggage and news are also uncountable.

questions.question_text: The plurals of criterion, analysis and datum are:
questions.explanation: These are irregular plurals from Latin and Greek.

questions.question_text: A pronoun is a word used:
questions.explanation: Types include personal, possessive, reflexive, relative and demonstrative.

questions.question_text: Choose: "Between you and ___, the plan will work."
questions.explanation: After a preposition, the object form "me" is used.

questions.question_text: Correct: "Me and him attended the meeting."
options: I and him attended the meeting.
Me and he attended the meeting.
He and I attended the meeting.
Him and me attended the meeting.
questions.explanation: Subject pronouns are required, and "I" comes last.

questions.question_text: A verb is a word that:
options: Expresses an action, state or occurrence
questions.explanation: Types include action, linking, auxiliary and modal verbs.

questions.question_text: A transitive verb differs from an intransitive verb in that a transitive verb:
options: Takes an object, e.g., "She wrote a report"
questions.explanation: "He arrived" is intransitive.

questions.question_text: Which is a modal verb?
questions.explanation: Modals include can, could, may, might, shall, should, will, would, must and ought to.

questions.question_text: The three forms of "write" are:
questions.explanation: It is an irregular verb.

questions.question_text: The three forms of "begin" are:
questions.explanation: Another irregular verb.

questions.question_text: The three forms of "choose" are:
questions.explanation: "Chosen" is the past participle.

questions.question_text: The three forms of "bring" are:
questions.explanation: The past tense and participle are the same.

questions.question_text: A phrasal verb is:
options: A verb combined with a preposition or adverb that gives a new meaning, e.g., "carry out"
questions.explanation: Other examples: give up and look after.

questions.question_text: Stative verbs such as "know" and "believe" are not used in the continuous form because they:
options: Describe states, not actions in progress
questions.explanation: "I am knowing" is incorrect.

questions.question_text: An adjective is a word that:
questions.explanation: Types include quality, quantity, number and demonstrative adjectives.

questions.question_text: The comparative and superlative of "good" are:
questions.explanation: It is an irregular adjective.

questions.question_text: The comparative and superlative of "bad" are:
questions.explanation: Irregular, like good and little.

questions.question_text: The comparative and superlative of "little" are:
questions.explanation: It is used for quantity.

questions.question_text: The correct order of adjectives is:
questions.explanation: Order: opinion, size, age, shape, colour, material.

questions.question_text: An adverb is a word that:
options: Modifies a verb, an adjective or another adverb
questions.explanation: Types: manner, time, place, frequency and degree.

questions.question_text: "Hard" differs from "hardly" in that "hard" means _____ and "hardly" means _____:
questions.explanation: "He works hard" versus "He hardly works".

questions.question_text: A preposition is a word that:
options: Shows the relation of a noun or pronoun to another word, e.g., "in the morning", "on Monday"
questions.explanation: Time: at, on, in; place: in, on, under.

tests.title: Unit 1: Introduction to English Grammar – Practice Test 2

questions.question_text: Fill in: "He has been working here ___ 2019."
questions.explanation: "Since" is used with a point in time.

questions.question_text: Fill in: "She is good ___ mathematics."
questions.explanation: The fixed phrase is "good at".

questions.question_text: Fill in: "The manager is different ___ his predecessor."
questions.explanation: The standard preposition is "different from".

questions.question_text: Fill in: "We divided the profit ___ the three partners."
questions.explanation: "Between" is for two, "among" for more than two.

questions.question_text: A conjunction is a word that:
questions.explanation: Types: coordinating, subordinating and correlative.

questions.question_text: Combine using "although": "He was tired. He finished the report."
options: Although he finished the report, he was tired.
Although he was tired, he finished the report.
He was tired although, he finished the report.
Although he was tired, but he finished the report.
questions.explanation: "Although" cannot be used with "but".

questions.question_text: Combine using "either…or": "Send an email. Call the client."
options: Either send an email nor call the client.
Either send an email, or not call the client.
Either send an email or call the client.
Send either an email and call the client.
questions.explanation: "Either" pairs with "or".

questions.question_text: Conjunctive adverbs include:
questions.explanation: They link independent clauses and need a semicolon or full stop before them.

questions.question_text: We use "an" before:
options: A vowel sound, e.g., "an hour" and "an MBA"
questions.explanation: The sound matters, not the spelling.

questions.question_text: The article is omitted before:
options: Plural and uncountable nouns used in a general sense, and names of most people
questions.explanation: E.g., "Honesty is the best policy".

questions.question_text: The twelve tenses are formed by combining:
options: Past, present and future with simple, continuous, perfect and perfect continuous aspects
questions.explanation: 3 times × 4 aspects = 12.

questions.question_text: The structure of the present perfect tense is:
questions.explanation: "She has completed the report."

questions.question_text: The simple past differs from the present perfect in that the simple past:
options: Refers to a completed action at a definite past time, while the present perfect links the past to the present
questions.explanation: "I saw him yesterday" versus "I have seen him".

questions.question_text: Fill in: "She has lived in Pune ___ ten years."
questions.explanation: "For" is used with a period; "since" with a point in time like 2015.

questions.question_text: Correct: "I have seen him yesterday."
questions.explanation: The present perfect is not used with a definite past time.

questions.question_text: Correct: "He go to the office by bus."
options: He is go to the office by bus.
He goes to the office by bus.
He gone to the office by bus.
He going to the office by bus.
questions.explanation: A third-person singular subject takes "-s".

questions.question_text: Correct: "I am knowing him for long."
options: I have known him for long.
I was knowing him for long.
I am known him for long.
questions.explanation: "Know" is stative and used in the perfect tense here.

questions.question_text: Correct (reported speech): "She said that she is busy."
options: She said that she has been busy.
She said that she will be busy.
She said that she were busy.
She said that she was busy.
questions.explanation: The tense backshifts after a past reporting verb.

questions.question_text: The sequence of tenses means that:
options: A past tense in the main clause is usually followed by a past form in the subordinate clause
questions.explanation: "I thought he was honest."

questions.question_text: The past continuous tense is used to:
options: Describe an action in progress at a past moment, e.g., "I was working at 8 pm"
Describe a habit in the present
questions.explanation: Structure: was/were + verb + ing.

questions.question_text: The rule of subject–verb agreement is:
options: The verb agrees with the object
A singular subject takes a singular verb and a plural subject takes a plural verb
questions.explanation: Check the real subject.

questions.question_text: Choose: "The news ___ shocking."
questions.explanation: "News" is an uncountable noun treated as singular.

questions.question_text: Choose: "Each of the employees ___ a locker."
questions.explanation: "Each" takes a singular verb.

questions.question_text: Choose: "A number of students ___ absent."
questions.explanation: "A number of" takes a plural verb.

questions.question_text: Choose: "The number of students ___ increasing."
questions.explanation: "The number of" takes a singular verb.

questions.question_text: Choose: "Neither the manager nor the employees ___ present."
questions.explanation: With neither…nor, the verb agrees with the nearer subject.

questions.question_text: Choose: "The committee ___ decided to extend the deadline."
questions.explanation: A collective noun acting as a unit takes a singular verb.

questions.question_text: Choose: "Ten lakh rupees ___ a large amount."
questions.explanation: A sum of money is treated as a single amount.

tests.title: Unit 1: Introduction to English Grammar – Practice Test 3

questions.question_text: Choose: "The manager, along with his team, ___ attending."
questions.explanation: "Along with" does not make the subject plural.

questions.question_text: Choose: "Mathematics ___ my favourite subject."
questions.explanation: Names of subjects ending in -s take singular verbs.

questions.question_text: Choose: "Bread and butter ___ my breakfast."
questions.explanation: Two subjects forming one idea take a singular verb.

questions.question_text: A sentence is:
options: A group of words without meaning
A group of words that expresses a complete thought
questions.explanation: It has a subject and a predicate.

questions.question_text: A phrase differs from a clause in that a phrase:
options: Has no subject–verb pair, while a clause does
questions.explanation: "In the morning" is a phrase.

questions.question_text: An independent clause:
options: Can stand alone as a sentence, while a dependent clause cannot
questions.explanation: A dependent clause begins with a subordinator such as "because".

questions.question_text: According to function, sentences are classified as:
questions.explanation: E.g., statement, question, command and exclamation.

questions.question_text: According to structure, sentences are classified as:
questions.explanation: They differ by the number and type of clauses.

questions.question_text: "Because it was raining, the match was cancelled" is a:
questions.explanation: It has one dependent and one independent clause.

questions.question_text: "The report was ready, but the client did not arrive" is a:
questions.explanation: Two independent clauses are joined by "but".

questions.question_text: "I stayed home because I was ill, and my sister cooked dinner" is a:
questions.explanation: Two independent clauses and one dependent clause.

questions.question_text: The six basic sentence patterns include:
options: S–V, S–V–O, S–V–C, S–V–IO–DO, S–V–O–C and S–V–A
questions.explanation: S = subject, V = verb, O = object, C = complement, A = adverbial.

questions.question_text: Parallel structure means:
options: Using different forms in a list
Using the same grammatical form for items in a list
questions.explanation: "She likes swimming, reading and cooking" is parallel.

questions.question_text: Correct: "She likes swimming, to read and cooking."
options: She likes swimming, reading and cooking.
She like swimming, reading and cooking.
She likes swimming, to read and to cook.
She likes to swim, reading and cooking.
questions.explanation: All items should use the -ing form.

questions.question_text: A sentence fragment is:
options: A group of words that lacks a subject or a complete verb, e.g., "Because he was late."
questions.explanation: It is corrected by adding a main clause.

questions.question_text: A run-on sentence is:
options: Two independent clauses joined without proper punctuation or a conjunction
questions.explanation: "He was late he missed the train" is a run-on.

questions.question_text: Correct the run-on: "He was late he missed the train."
options: He was late; and he missed the train.
He was late, so he missed the train.
He was late he, missed the train.
He was late, he missed the train.
questions.explanation: Use a conjunction or a semicolon.

questions.question_text: A comma splice is:
options: Joining two independent clauses with only a comma
questions.explanation: "The meeting ended, everyone left" is a splice.

questions.question_text: Correct the comma splice: "The meeting ended, everyone left."
questions.explanation: A semicolon or a full stop is needed.

questions.question_text: A dangling modifier is:
options: A modifier next to its noun
A modifier that does not clearly attach to the word it is meant to modify
questions.explanation: "Walking down the road, the bus hit him" is dangling.

questions.question_text: Correct the dangling modifier: "Walking down the road, the bus hit him."
options: While he was walking down the road, the bus hit him.
The bus hit him, walking down the road.
Walking, the bus hit him down the road.
Walking down the road, the bus hit him.
questions.explanation: The subject of the participle must be clear.

questions.question_text: A misplaced modifier is:
options: A modifier next to its word
A modifier placed far from the word it describes, creating confusion
questions.explanation: "She almost drove for two hours" is misplaced.

questions.question_text: Correct: "She almost drove for two hours."
options: She almost drove two for hours.
She drove for almost two hours.
She drove almost for two hours.
Almost she drove for two hours.
questions.explanation: "Almost" should modify "two hours".

questions.question_text: Redundancy means:
options: Using unnecessary words that repeat the meaning, e.g., "return back"
questions.explanation: It weakens business writing.

questions.question_text: Remove redundancy: "Please return back the free gift."
options: Please return the free gift back.
questions.explanation: "Return" already means "give back"; a gift is free.

questions.question_text: Passive: "The manager approved the plan."
options: The plan is approved by the manager.
The plan was approved by the manager.
The plan has been approved the manager.
The manager was approved by the plan.
questions.explanation: The past tense becomes "was + past participle".

questions.question_text: Passive: "The company will launch a new product."
options: A new product will launch by the company.
A new product would be launched the company.
A new product is launched by the company.
A new product will be launched by the company.
questions.explanation: Use "will be + past participle".

questions.question_text: Passive: "They are preparing the budget."
options: The budget was being prepared by them.
The budget is being prepared by them.
The budget is prepared by them.
The budget has been prepared by them.
questions.explanation: Present continuous becomes "is being + past participle".

tests.title: Unit 1: Introduction to English Grammar – Practice Test 4

questions.question_text: Passive: "She has written the report."
options: The report was written by her.
The report has been written by her.
The report had been written by her.
The report is written by her.
questions.explanation: Present perfect becomes "has been + past participle".

questions.question_text: Active: "The bill was paid by the client."
options: The client has paid the bill.
The client was paying the bill.
questions.explanation: Keep the same tense.

questions.question_text: The passive voice is preferred when:
options: The doer is unknown or unimportant, or the action matters more
questions.explanation: E.g., "The files were deleted."

questions.question_text: Indirect speech: He said, "I am busy."
options: He said that he will be busy.
He said that I was busy.
He said that he was busy.
He said that he is busy.
questions.explanation: The present tense becomes past.

questions.question_text: Indirect speech: She asked, "Where do you live?"
options: She asked where do I live.
She asked that where I lived.
questions.explanation: Reported questions use statement word order.

questions.question_text: Indirect speech: The manager said to us, "Submit the report by Monday."
options: The manager told us to submit the report by Monday.
The manager told us that submit the report by Monday.
The manager asked us submit the report by Monday.
The manager said us to submit the report by Monday.
questions.explanation: A command is reported with "told + to".

questions.question_text: Indirect speech: He said, "I will call you tomorrow."
options: He said that he will call you tomorrow.
He said that I would call him next day.
He said that he would call me the next day.
He said that he would call you tomorrow.
questions.explanation: "Will" becomes "would" and "tomorrow" becomes "the next day".

questions.question_text: Direct speech: She said that she had finished her work.
options: She said, "I had finished my work."
She said, "She had finished her work."
She said, "I have finished my work."
questions.explanation: Past perfect becomes present perfect and the pronoun changes.

questions.question_text: In reported speech, "now", "today", "here" and "yesterday" generally become:
options: soon, tonight, everywhere and last day
later, tomorrow, there and the next day
then, that day, there and the previous day
questions.explanation: Time and place words shift.

questions.question_text: The first conditional is used for:
options: A real or likely future situation, e.g., "If you pay today, we will deliver tomorrow"
questions.explanation: The structure is if + present, will + verb.

questions.question_text: Complete: "If I had known the price, I ___ the laptop."
questions.explanation: The third conditional uses if + past perfect, would have + past participle.

questions.question_text: Which sentence uses "must" for obligation in a business context?
questions.explanation: "Must" shows strong obligation.

questions.question_text: "May" differs from "might" in that "might":
options: Shows a more remote or less certain possibility
questions.explanation: "It may rain" is more likely than "it might rain".

questions.question_text: A comma is used to:
options: Join two independent clauses without a conjunction
Separate items in a list and after introductory phrases
questions.explanation: It also sets off non-essential clauses.

questions.question_text: A semicolon is used to:
options: Join two closely related independent clauses, e.g., "The report is ready; the client has not arrived."
questions.explanation: It can also separate complex list items.

questions.question_text: A colon is used to:
options: Introduce a list, explanation or quotation
questions.explanation: "Bring three things: ID, form and fee."

questions.question_text: Correct: "The companys policy is clear."
questions.explanation: An apostrophe + s shows possession for a singular noun.

questions.question_text: "Its" differs from "it's" in that "its" is _____ and "it's" is _____:
options: A possessive; short for "it is" or "it has"
questions.explanation: "The company changed its policy; it's effective today."

questions.question_text: Punctuate correctly: "however the committee agreed to the proposal"
options: However; the committee agreed to the proposal.
However the committee agreed, to the proposal.
However the committee, agreed to the proposal.
However, the committee agreed to the proposal.
questions.explanation: A comma follows the introductory "however".

questions.question_text: Punctuate correctly: "she asked are you coming to the meeting"
options: She asked are you coming to the meeting.
She asked, "are you coming to the meeting."
She asked "Are you coming to the meeting".
She asked, "Are you coming to the meeting?"
questions.explanation: Use a comma, quotation marks and a question mark.

questions.question_text: "Affect" is usually a _____ and "effect" is usually a _____:
questions.explanation: "The delay will affect sales; the effect was clear."

questions.question_text: "Principal" differs from "principle" in that "principal" means _____ and "principle" means _____:
options: Chief or head; a rule or belief
questions.explanation: "The principal gave a principle-based speech."

questions.question_text: "Advice" is a _____ and "advise" is a _____:
questions.explanation: "I advise you to take his advice."

questions.question_text: "Ensure", "insure" and "assure" mean respectively:
options: To make certain; to cover with insurance; to promise or reassure
To reassure; to cover; to promise
To promise; to make certain; to cover
To cover; to promise; to make certain
questions.explanation: "Ensure quality, insure the goods, assure the client."

questions.question_text: Capital letters are used for:
options: The first word of a sentence, proper nouns and the pronoun "I"
questions.explanation: Also days, months and titles before names.

questions.question_text: Rewrite concisely: "Due to the fact that the market was down, we had to postpone the launch."
options: Due to the fact that the market was down, we postponed the launch.
Because of the fact that the market was down, we had to postpone it.
The market being down, the launch postponement was had.
Because the market was down, we postponed the launch.
questions.explanation: "Due to the fact that" can be replaced by "because".

questions.question_text: Grammatical accuracy is important in business communication because it:
options: Builds credibility, avoids misunderstanding and projects professionalism
questions.explanation: Errors can damage trust and cause costly mistakes.
